AIMA · Chapter 9

Inference in First-Order Logic

Russell & Norvig — Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach, 4th ed.

// Chapter 9 at a Glance

Chapter 8 gave us the language of first-order logic. Chapter 9 asks: how do we actually draw conclusions from a FOL knowledge base? Three broad approaches are covered, each with different trade-offs in completeness, efficiency, and practical applicability.

// Three Inference Approaches

ApproachCore IdeaComplete?Best For
Propositionalization Reduce FOL to propositional logic via instantiation, then use prop. inference ✅ (by Herbrand's theorem) Small finite domains
Forward / Backward Chaining Apply Generalized Modus Ponens to definite clauses using unification ✅ for definite clauses (semi-decidable for full FOL) Datalog, production systems, Prolog
Resolution Refutation Convert KB + ¬query to CNF, resolve until □ (empty clause) ✅ (refutation complete) Theorem proving, hardware/software verification

Key Vocabulary

  • Substitution θ — mapping from variables to terms
  • SUBST(θ, α) — apply θ to expression α
  • Unifier — θ such that SUBST(θ,p) = SUBST(θ,q)
  • MGU — most general unifier (least-committing)
  • Definite clause — exactly one positive literal
  • Datalog — function-free definite clauses (decidable)
  • Horn clause — at most one positive literal

Decidability Notes

  • Full FOL entailment: semi-decidable — can confirm theorems but may loop on non-theorems
  • Datalog (function-free): decidable in polynomial time
  • Propositional logic: decidable (co-NP-complete)
  • Prolog: adds closed-world assumption + negation-as-failure → not purely logical, but practical

// Propositionalization: The Naive Approach

Every universally quantified sentence can be instantiated with every ground term in the KB (Universal Instantiation). Every existentially quantified sentence introduces a new Skolem constant (Existential Instantiation). The resulting propositionalized KB can then be handed to any propositional inference procedure.

Why It's Usually Slow

If there are n constant symbols and rules with k variables, there are nk instantiations per rule. With function symbols the Herbrand universe is infinite, requiring iterative deepening over term depth.

-- Universal Instantiation (UI) -- For every variable v and ground term g: SUBST({v/g}, α) follows from ∀v α -- Example: ∀x King(x) ⇒ Greedy(x) + ground terms: John, Richard, Father(John) → King(John) ⇒ Greedy(John) → King(Richard) ⇒ Greedy(Richard) → King(Father(John)) ⇒ Greedy(Father(John)) ... (and so on for every ground term)

// Unification

Unification finds a substitution θ that makes two expressions syntactically identical. It eliminates the need to propositionalize — we can work directly with variables. The Most General Unifier (MGU) is the least-committed substitution; any other unifier is an instance of the MGU.

// Fig 9.1 — UNIFY Algorithm

Fig 9.1 — The UNIFY algorithm. Recursively matches terms element by element, building up substitution θ.

Key Cases

  • If both are the same constant/symbol → return current θ (already unified)
  • If one is a variable → call UNIFY-VAR
  • If both are compound → unify operators, then recursively unify argument lists
  • Otherwise → return failure

Occur Check

UNIFY-VAR checks whether var already appears in x before binding. Without this, {x/F(x)} would cause infinite expansion. The occur check makes unification O(n²) in the worst case; many systems skip it for efficiency.

// Unification Examples

Expression 1Expression 2MGU
Knows(John, x)Knows(John, Jane){x/Jane}
Knows(John, x)Knows(y, Bill){x/Bill, y/John}
Knows(John, x)Knows(x, Elizabeth){x/John} → Knows(John,Elizabeth)? No — x binds to John but then Knows(John,John)≠Knows(John,Elizabeth)
Knows(John, x)Knows(y, Mother(y)){y/John, x/Mother(John)}
Knows(John, x)Knows(x, Elizabeth)failure — x cannot simultaneously be John and Elizabeth

// Fig 9.2 — Subsumption Lattices

Fig 9.2 — (a) Lattice for Employs(IBM, Richard). (b) Lattice for Employs(John, John). More specific sentences appear lower in the lattice.

The subsumption lattice shows how sentences relate via substitution. A more specific sentence (fewer free variables) sits below a more general one. The MGU finds the lowest node that satisfies both expressions.

// Generalized Modus Ponens

The "lifted" version of Modus Ponens works directly on FOL sentences by using unification rather than full instantiation:

-- Generalized Modus Ponens -- Given: p₁', p₂', ..., pₙ' (known facts) -- Rule: (p₁ ∧ p₂ ∧ ... ∧ pₙ ⇒ q) -- where SUBST(θ, pᵢ') = SUBST(θ, pᵢ) for all i -- Conclude: SUBST(θ, q) -- Example: -- Known: Missile(M₁), Owns(Nono, M₁) -- Rule: Missile(x) ∧ Owns(Nono, x) ⇒ Sells(West, x, Nono) -- θ = {x/M₁} -- Conclude: Sells(West, M₁, Nono)

// Forward Chaining

Forward chaining starts from known facts and fires matching rules repeatedly until the goal is derived or no new facts can be inferred. It is data-driven: the engine doesn't know in advance what it's looking for — it simply applies all applicable rules until done.

// Fig 9.3 — FOL-FC-ASK Algorithm

Fig 9.3 — FOL-FC-ASK: Forward chaining algorithm for first-order definite clauses. Each iteration adds newly inferred atomic sentences to the KB.

How It Works

  • Each iteration: find all rules whose premises unify with known facts
  • Apply the substitution to the rule's conclusion and add to KB
  • Variables are standardized apart to avoid conflicts across rule applications
  • Stops when query unifies with something in KB, or when no new facts are produced (fixpoint)

// Fig 9.4 — Crime Example: Forward Chaining Proof Tree

Fig 9.4 — Proof tree for the crime example. Initial ground facts at the bottom; derived facts built upward in two iterations.

Click each fact/rule below to see what role it plays in the derivation:

// Click any fact or rule to inspect
American(West) Missile(M₁) Owns(Nono, M₁) Enemy(Nono, America) Rule 1: Missile ∧ Owns → Sells Rule 2: Missile → Weapon Rule 3: Enemy → Hostile Rule 4: American ∧ Weapon ∧ Sells ∧ Hostile → Criminal → Sells(West, M₁, Nono) → Weapon(M₁) → Hostile(Nono) ⊢ Criminal(West)

// Fig 9.5 — Datalog: Map Coloring Example

Fig 9.5 — Australia map-coloring expressed as a single definite clause in Datalog. Regions are constants; Diff encodes adjacency constraints.

Properties of Datalog

  • No function symbols → finite Herbrand base → decidable
  • Forward chaining runs in polynomial time on Datalog KBs
  • Used in deductive databases and modern systems like Datomic
  • Semi-naive evaluation: only process newly added facts each iteration

// Backward Chaining

Backward chaining is goal-driven: start from the query and work backward, finding rules whose conclusions match, then trying to prove those rules' premises. It only explores paths relevant to the goal — making it much more efficient than forward chaining for targeted queries.

// Fig 9.6 — FOL-BC-ASK Algorithm

Fig 9.6 — FOL-BC-ASK: A simple backward-chaining algorithm. FOL-BC-OR finds rules matching the goal; FOL-BC-AND proves all conjuncts in a rule's body.

Algorithm Structure

  • FOL-BC-OR: for a goal, find all rules whose head unifies with it; try each
  • FOL-BC-AND: prove all conjuncts in a rule's body; pass bindings left to right
  • Returns a generator of substitutions — multiple solutions possible
  • Depth-first search over the AND-OR proof tree

// Fig 9.7 — Crime Example: Backward Chaining Proof Tree

Fig 9.7 — Backward chaining from Criminal(West). Substitution bindings are shown; once z binds to Nono, all subsequent subgoals use this binding.

// Forward vs. Backward Chaining

PropertyForward ChainingBackward Chaining
DirectionData-driven (facts → goal)Goal-driven (goal → facts)
CompletenessComplete for definite clausesComplete for definite clauses
EfficiencyCan derive many irrelevant factsFocuses on subgoals relevant to query
RedundancyDetects duplicate facts easilyMay re-prove same subgoal many times
LoopsTerminates (fixpoint)Can loop on recursive rules
ApplicationsDeductive databases, production systems, monitoringProlog, expert systems, planning

// Resolution: Complete Inference for Full FOL

Resolution is a single inference rule that, combined with CNF conversion, yields a refutation-complete proof system for full first-order logic. To prove α from KB, we show that KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable by deriving the empty clause □.

// CNF Conversion: Step by Step

// The Resolution Rule

-- FOL Resolution Rule -- Given two clauses (disjunctions of literals): -- ℓ₁ ∨ ... ∨ ℓₖ ∨ m (contains positive literal m) -- m₁ ∨ ... ∨ mₙ ∨ ¬m' (contains negative literal ¬m') -- where UNIFY(m, m') = θ -- Produce the resolvent: -- SUBST(θ, ℓ₁ ∨ ... ∨ ℓₖ ∨ m₁ ∨ ... ∨ mₙ) -- Factoring: merge two unifiable literals in the same clause -- before resolving. Required for completeness.

// Fig 9.10 — Resolution Proof: West is a Criminal

Fig 9.10 — Resolution proof of Criminal(West). At each step, the unifying literals are in bold; the positive-literal clause is shaded blue.

// Fig 9.11 — Resolution Proof: Curiosity Killed the Cat

Fig 9.11 — Resolution proof that Curiosity killed Tuna. Note the use of factoring to derive Loves(G(Jack),Jack), and careful standardization of variables apart.

// Resolution Search Strategies

StrategyDescriptionComplete?
Breadth-firstExplore all clauses of depth d before d+1✅ Yes
Unit resolutionAt least one parent must be a unit clause (single literal)❌ Incomplete for full FOL
Set of supportOne parent must descend from the negated goal✅ Yes
Input resolutionOne parent must be an input clause (from original KB)❌ Incomplete
Linear resolutionOne parent is always the most recent resolvent✅ Yes
SubsumptionDiscard clauses subsumed by an existing clause✅ (pruning only)

// Equality and Demodulation

Equality requires special treatment. Naively adding symmetry, reflexivity, and transitivity axioms is very expensive. Two alternatives:

-- Demodulation (rewriting): replace term with equal term -- If we know Father(Macbeth) = Duncan and have P(Father(Macbeth)): -- → can produce P(Duncan) directly -- Paramodulation: generalization using unification -- If we know t = s and clause contains term t' unifiable with t: -- → substitute s for the unified term in the clause -- Yields a complete procedure for handling equality
